paragraphs: There are different kinds of death. In some, the body remains; in others, it disappears completely along with the spirit. This usually happens only when a person is alone, for such is God’s will. As no one sees the end, we say the person is lost or has gone on a long journey—which, indeed, they have. But sometimes it has happened in sight of many people, as abundant testimony shows. In one kind of death, the spirit dies too. This has been known to happen even while the body remains vigorous for many years. Sometimes, as reliable witnesses testify, the spirit dies with the body, but after a time rises again in the place where the body decayed.

I was considering these words of Hali—may God give him rest—and questioning their full meaning. I had a glimmer of understanding, but wondered whether something lay behind what I had grasped. So absorbed was I that I did not notice where I had wandered until a sudden cold wind struck my face and made me aware of my surroundings again. To my astonishment, everything looked unfamiliar. On every side stretched a bleak, desolate plain, overgrown with tall, dry grass. It rustled and whistled in the autumn wind, suggesting heaven knows what mysterious, unsettling things. Far apart, strangely shaped, dark-coloured rocks rose above it. They seemed to understand one another and exchange looks of troubling significance, as though they had raised their heads to watch the outcome of some event they had foreseen. A few dead, damaged trees here and there seemed to lead this evil conspiracy of silent expectation.

I thought it must be late in the day, although I could not see the sun. I knew the air was raw and cold, but that awareness was in my mind rather than my body. I felt no discomfort. Low, lead-coloured clouds hung over the whole dismal landscape like a visible curse. Everything held a threat and an omen—a hint of evil, a suggestion of doom. There was no bird, animal or insect. The wind sighed through the bare branches of the dead trees, and the grey grass bent to whisper its dreadful secret to the earth. But no other sound or movement disturbed the terrible stillness of that gloomy place.

Among the grass I noticed several weathered stones, clearly shaped with tools. They were broken, moss-covered and half sunk in the earth. Some lay flat; others leaned at different angles; none stood upright. They were plainly gravestones, although the graves themselves no longer formed either mounds or hollows. The years had levelled everything. Larger blocks scattered here and there marked places where some pompous tomb or ambitious monument had once raised its feeble challenge to oblivion. These relics looked so old, these remains of vanity and memorials of love and devotion. They were so battered, worn and stained, and the place so neglected, deserted and forgotten, that I could not help thinking I had discovered the burial ground of a prehistoric people whose very name had long since vanished.

Absorbed in these thoughts, I paid no attention for a while to how my own experiences had led here. But soon I wondered, “How did I come here?” A moment’s reflection seemed to make everything clear. It also explained, though disturbingly, the strange qualities my imagination had given to everything I saw and heard. I was ill. I now remembered that a sudden fever had laid me low. My family had told me that, when delirious, I constantly cried out for freedom and air, and had to be held in bed to keep me from escaping outdoors. Now I had slipped past the people watching me and wandered here—to where? I could not guess. Clearly, I was a considerable distance from the city where I lived—the ancient and famous city of Carcosa.

There was no sign of human life to see or hear. No rising smoke, no watchdog barking, no cattle lowing, no children shouting at play—nothing but that dismal burial ground, whose air of mystery and dread came from my own disordered brain. Was I becoming delirious again, out here beyond anyone’s help? Was it all, in fact, an illusion of my madness? I called out the names of my wives and sons and stretched out my hands to find theirs, even as I walked among the crumbling stones and withered grass.

A noise behind me made me turn. A wild animal—a lynx—was approaching. I thought: If I collapse here in this wasteland, if the fever returns and I weaken, this animal will be at my throat. I sprang towards it, shouting. It trotted calmly past, within a hand’s width of me, and disappeared behind a rock.

A moment later, a man’s head seemed to rise from the ground a short distance away. He was climbing the far side of a low hill whose top barely rose above the surrounding land. Soon his whole figure appeared against the grey clouds. He was half naked, half clothed in skins. His hair was uncombed, his beard long and ragged. In one hand he carried a bow and arrow. In the other he held a blazing torch that trailed a long stream of black smoke. He walked slowly and cautiously, as if afraid of falling into an open grave hidden by the tall grass. This strange figure surprised me but did not frighten me. I changed direction to intercept him and met him almost face to face, addressing him with the familiar greeting, “God keep you.”
He paid no attention and did not slow his pace.
“Good stranger,” I continued, “I am ill and lost. Please, I beg you, show me the way to Carcosa.”
The man broke into a savage chant in an unknown language and passed on into the distance.

An owl hooted mournfully from the branch of a decaying tree, and another answered far away. Looking up, I saw Aldebaran and the Hyades through a sudden gap in the clouds! Everything suggested night—the lynx, the man with the torch, the owl. Yet I could see—I could even see the stars without any darkness. I saw, but apparently could neither be seen nor heard. Under what terrible spell was I living?

I sat at the foot of a great tree to think seriously about what I should do. I could no longer doubt that I was mad, yet I recognised a reason for doubt in that very certainty. I had no trace of fever. I also felt an unfamiliar exhilaration and energy, an uplifting of both mind and body. All my senses seemed alert. I could feel the air as a heavy substance. I could hear the silence.

As I sat leaning against the trunk of the giant tree, I saw that one of its great roots gripped a stone slab. Part of the slab stuck out into a hollow formed by another root. This partly sheltered the stone from the weather, although it had badly decayed. Its edges had worn round, its corners were eaten away, and its surface was deeply grooved and flaking. Glittering particles of mica lay in the earth around it, remnants of its decay. Apparently the stone had marked the grave from which the tree had sprung ages ago. The tree’s demanding roots had robbed the grave and taken the stone prisoner.

A sudden gust blew some dry leaves and twigs off the stone’s upper face. I saw the shallow raised letters of an inscription and bent to read it. God in Heaven! My full name! The date of my birth! The date of my death!

As I sprang to my feet in terror, a horizontal shaft of light lit the whole side of the tree. The sun was rising in the pink east. I stood between the tree and its broad red disc—no shadow darkened the trunk!

A chorus of wolves howled a greeting to the dawn. I saw them sitting on their haunches, alone and in groups, on the tops of uneven mounds and burial heaps. These filled half my view of the wasteland and stretched to the horizon. And then I knew they were the ruins of the ancient and famous city of Carcosa.
These are the facts given to the medium Bayrolles by the spirit Hoseib Alar Robardin.
